item.title: China's industrial output growth picks up in August as high-tech, robot output gains
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on China's economic performance in August 2026 in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 15, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Yuwei) BEIJING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- China's value-added industrial output expanded 5.2 percent year on year in August, accelerating by 0.7 percentage point from the previous month, official data showed Tuesday, with industrial robots among the standout products. High-tech manufacturing output jumped 16.7 percent year on year in August, while equipment manufacturing rose 12.1 percent, outpacing overall industrial output growth by 11.5 and 6.9 percentage points, respectively, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS). At the product level, output of industrial robots jumped 34.6 percent year on year in August, while lithium-ion batteries and 3D printing equipment saw increases of 57.2 percent and 29.9 percent, respectively. The rapid growth comes as industrial robots are finding applications across a widening array of industries in China. Data released in July by the China Machinery Industry Federation showed that homegrown industrial robots are now used in 253 industry groups, covering more than half of all such groups nationwide. In terms of broader sectors, the value-added output of the mining sector fell 1.4 percent year on year, while that of the manufacturing sector grew 6.1 percent. The value-added output of the electricity, heat, gas and water production and supply sectors rose 4.9 percent. Looking at ownership, the value-added output of state-owned and state-holding enterprises grew 3 percent year on year, while that of private enterprises rose 3.7 percent. In the first eight months of 2026, industrial output grew 5.3 percent year on year, data revealed. NBS data also showed that the purchasing managers' index for China's manufacturing sector in August stood at 49.8, while the index measuring firms' expectations for production and business activity came in at 53.8, signaling continued confidence in the outlook. From January to July, total profits of China's major industrial firms reached 4.58 trillion yuan (about 677.12 billion U.S. dollars), up 17.6 percent year on year. Industrial output is used to measure the activity of large enterprises each with an annual main business revenue of at least 20 million yuan. Fu Linghui, an NBS spokesperson, told a press conference on Tuesday that industrial production remained stable in August despite volatility in global energy and raw material markets, supported by efforts to secure energy supplies and advance the green transition. He added that emerging industries continued to gain momentum as technological and industrial innovation became more integrated, with new growth drivers contributing more than 60 percent of the increase in industrial output. ■

item.title: Xi Story: Making canals channels for connectivity, prosperity, better life
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
NANNING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Sitting in a glass case at a museum in south China's Qinzhou, a glazed porcelain bowl etched with a floral pattern offers a tantalizing clue to this coastal city's maritime-trade past. Despite being centuries old, the bowl bears scarcely any signs of use. Experts believe that the bowl, instead of being made for use in local households, was likely among the merchandise stockpiled for trade during the Song Dynasty (960-1279), when sugar and ceramics were shipped from Qinzhou to Southeast Asian countries along the Maritime Silk Road. A historic port city on the coast of the Beibu Gulf in the South China Sea, Qinzhou, located in Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, is gaining fresh momentum as a maritime hub with the opening of the Pinglu Canal, a major river-to-sea canal project set to become operational on Wednesday. The canal stretches along the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, a strategic trade route connecting China's inland regions with ASEAN and other global markets. During an inspection tour of Guangxi in December 2023, Chinese President Xi Jinping was briefed on the construction progress of the canal in front of a sand-table model. Guangxi's future growth potential lies in connecting its waterways to the sea and realizing integrated river-sea transport, Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, said during that trip. He added that Guangxi should strengthen itself via maritime development, noting that the region has both a strong need and great potential to further expand opening up, both internally and externally. Running from north to south, the Pinglu Canal links the Xijiang River shipping route with the Beibu Gulf. It is expected to shorten the shipping distance between China's southwestern hinterland and ASEAN, China's largest trading partner, by 560 km and reduce logistics costs by 18 to 30 percent, according to Lu Xinning, vice chairperson of the regional government of Guangxi. China's natural river systems generally run from west to east toward the sea, making it difficult to rely on existing rivers and lakes to connect the country's north and south. China has a long history of building canals. The best-known is the more than 2,500-year-old Grand Canal, the world's oldest and longest artificial waterway system, and a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2014. Xi has attached great importance to the protection and revitalization of the Grand Canal. He once stressed that the Grand Canal is a "precious heritage passed down to us by our ancestors." In 2006, when he was secretary of the CPC Zhejiang Provincial Committee, he took a "water bus" along a section of the Grand Canal in the provincial capital Hangzhou to inspect cleanup and revitalization of the canal. The "water bus" passenger service, launched in 2004, was the first of its kind along an urban Grand Canal network. Along the way, Xi asked in detail about everything from waterway network protection and shipping operations to the development of scenic areas along the canal. He encouraged Hangzhou officials to turn the canal into "a canal for the people" and "a canal for visitors," stressing that the people should be the ultimate beneficiaries. His attention to the Grand Canal has remained unchanged over the years. In November 2020, as China's top leader, Xi visited the eastern city of Yangzhou, where some of the waterway system's oldest sections are located. "For centuries, the canal has nourished the cities and people along its banks, bringing prosperity and well-being to them," he said. "I hope everyone will work together to protect the Grand Canal and ensure that it continues to benefit the people for generations to come," he told local officials and residents. Yangzhou, described by Xi as a "wonderful place built along the water, thriving on it and made beautiful by it," is a vivid example of how the Grand Canal has nourished a city and shaped its fortunes. Just like Yangzhou, Qinzhou today is poised to reap the benefits of greater connectivity -- this time, connectivity from river to sea, thanks to the Pinglu Canal. The Pinglu Canal is bringing to life the historical tradition of the Grand Canal in a new era, a tradition of fostering prosperity through waterways, said Xie Zhujun, a researcher with the Guangxi Academy of Social Sciences. Ultimately, the purpose of a canal is to improve people's livelihoods and deliver broader economic and social benefits, he noted. For Ning Qiongri, a Qinzhou native and a vlogger who has posted some 1,600 videos chronicling the construction of the Pinglu Canal, the project promises not only greater prosperity, but also a better life for local people. "Many people find jobs thanks to the canal's construction. I've also seen brand-new villages and schools built along its banks, as well as supermarkets and restaurants that are eager to name themselves after the canal," Ning revealed. ■

item.title: Xinhua Commentary: Strategic, long-term vision needed for China-India ties
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
BEIJING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- The recent meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi produced important consensus and marked the two leaders' reaffirmation of the growth of China-India ties after they guided the bilateral relations from starting afresh to making further improvements since 2024. The most important consensus reached during the meeting on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi is that China and India should be partners. It was the third meeting between the two leaders in three years. As Xi noted during their talks, to promote the steady and sustained development of China-India relations, both sides need to calibrate the direction with an objective and rational strategic perception, help each other succeed in the spirit of win-win cooperation, remove irritants with the political wisdom of mutual respect and mutual understanding, and contribute to a better world with open and inclusive multilateral coordination. China has always viewed and developed its relations with India from a strategic height and with a long-term view. As two major ancient civilizations, China and India should demonstrate sufficient wisdom and capacity to maintain and develop their bilateral ties. Over the centuries, the peoples of the two neighboring countries have developed precious bonds via exchanges and mutual learning. In modern times, the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence -- specified by the Chinese leadership in their entirety for the first time -- were included in the China-India and China-Myanmar joint statements that called for making them basic norms for state-to-state relations, which is an outstanding contribution to the international system. The two countries should treasure and carry forward the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, and pursue parallel progress in developing bilateral ties and solving border issues with the two tracks reinforcing each other, to maintain peace and tranquility in border areas and advance long-term development of bilateral relations. China and India are the world's two most populous countries. The essence of their relationship lies in how two major developing countries with a population of over 1.4 billion each can get along with each other. The two countries offer each other development opportunities, not threats. This strategic judgment is based on the development stages of the two countries and the international environment, and serves the common interests of both countries and their peoples. Both countries are in a critical period of their respective national modernization drives, and development is the biggest common denominator. The two countries are partners for cooperation, not rivals. Both sides should draw on each other's strengths and develop together. As major members of the Global South, China and India shoulder the international responsibility of setting an example in seeking strength through unity for developing countries, and contributing to advancing world multipolarity and the democratization of international relations. Both countries should work together to advance high-quality development of greater BRICS cooperation and provide more positive energy for global peace, stability, development and prosperity. It is expected that China and India will maintain the right direction in the development of their relationship, advance exchanges and cooperation in various fields, promote the steady and sustained development of bilateral ties, and make due contributions to the cause of human progress. ■

item.title: Xi urges Chinese police to remain committed to serving people with responsibility, dedication
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
BEIJING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping has called on the country's police officers to remain committed to serving the people, be loyal guardians of the Party and the people, and demonstrate a strong sense of responsibility and dedication. Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks in a reply letter to a primary-level police force from Zhangzhou, east China's Fujian Province. In his letter to the "Zhangzhou 110" police unit, Xi lauded its police officers for their dedication and hard work at the grassroots level in serving the public and maintaining social stability for the people. He emphasized that the police bear the important responsibility of safeguarding the people's well-being and the country's peace, calling on Chinese police to uphold fine traditions, devote themselves to wholeheartedly addressing the needs and concerns of the people, and work diligently to protect the safety of the public. The "Zhangzhou 110" unit is one of the exemplary primary-level units within China's police forces. Since 1990, it has pioneered and continuously improved a rapid response mechanism tied to the 110 police emergency call service, playing a significant role in combating crime, maintaining public security, and serving the community. During his tenure in Fujian, Xi visited the police unit three times to inspect and guide its work. Recently, members of the unit wrote to Xi, reporting on their work and expressing their determination to fulfill duties on the new journey. ■

item.title: China's robots advance from stage to shop floor
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-14
BEIJING, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- A robotic hand picked up a calligraphy brush, dipped it in ink and wrote "fu," a Chinese character meaning good fortune, on a square of red paper, delighting crowds. Chinese robots like this one are no longer just event performers. They are increasingly clocking in for real work, and an entire industry is forming around teaching them how. FROM GALA STAGE TO CONVENIENCE POD At the China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS), which ended Sunday in Beijing, Galbot G1, which went viral after folding laundry in a video clip for this year's globally broadcasted Spring Festival Gala, staffed an unmanned convenience pod. Such pods are already operating at sites including Beijing's Summer Palace, a former imperial garden, where each is expected to serve more than 1,000 visitors a day. The first overseas store of this type opened in Hong Kong on Sept. 1. Robots are also being deployed in other jobs. At an "unstaffed post office" booth, a robot stamps postcards, drops them into a mailbox, then fetches blind-box toys for customers. A few meters away, a pancake robot flips crepes to order, while a coffee robot pours latte art onto a fresh cup. "We have a coffee-making robot on campus, but these are more advanced," said visitor Olga, a Belarusian professor at Beijing Foreign Studies University. It takes humans considerable effort to create latte art, she added, but robots do it with ease. CLOSING THE TRAINING GAP For all the novelty, a wide gap remains between demonstration and deployment: training. "China's domestic shipments of humanoid robots reached 23,000 units in the first half of this year, but fewer than 5 percent are working stably on real production lines," said Zhu Kai, head of the Shijingshan Embodied Intelligence Training Center. Production lines are far messier than a stage. "High-quality, multimodal real-robot data fit for industrial training doesn't reach even 1 percent of actual demand," Zhu said, adding that the shortage is the core obstacle to moving robots "from performing to actually working." Closing that gap starts in a "vocational school" for robots. The training center, a short walk from the CIFTIS fairground at Shougang Park, is where much of the "homework" gets done. Nearly 270 robots work there at full capacity on chores, caregiving drills and factory tasks such as automatically placing circuit boards onto a production line, producing nearly 20 million high-quality data entries a year. The "school" opened its doors to visitors during the fair, and the lessons translate into human-like movements: rows of robots practiced fetching and setting down boxes or ironing trousers, each following a human mentor demonstrating the moves. Those mentors now have an official title. On the fair's opening day, Sept. 9, China formally recognized a new occupation: embodied-intelligence robot application technicians, with two new trades within it -- robot data collectors and robot trainers. The tools are changing, too. Data collectors once puppeteered machines from fixed lab consoles. But with new capture rigs mounted, they can now easily enter real-world work scenarios, recording human hands at work. At one booth, VR maker NOLO displayed its EgoCapture, a head-mounted rig that records 360 degrees of real human operations. Wear it on a trail run, and it generates exactly the data a robot would need to judge a long-distance turn. Clients can buy the service instead of the full set of gear. Other booths harvest the rest of a robot's education: tactile sensors from Tashan Technology capture the sensation and force of a grip, while dexterous hands from CasiaHand Robotics -- with a built-in "brain" model -- learn to act on their own. The output of this schooling shows up on the fairground itself: much of the training data behind the exhibits in the fair came from the center, said Zhu. DATA ON THE MARKET Data itself is becoming a commodity, and this year's CIFTIS fair gave it a pathway to cross borders. At a forum, the fair launched China's first industry-level platform aiming to provide international service for embodied-intelligence data, built by Beijing Shijingshan Science and Technology Innovation Group in partnership with China Telecom's Beijing branch. The groundwork has been established in the Shijingshan district of Beijing: China's first 3D high-quality dataset for large-model training has been registered, four data service stations have opened, and more than 200 data products have been listed, while Beijing as a whole aims for 100 high-quality industrial datasets by 2028. "The government sets the stage, and the companies perform. CIFTIS works like an amplifier, turning Beijing's industrial strengths into international cooperation opportunities," Zhu said. The robots are already earning their keep with overseas deployment. Anyverse Dynamics, a Beijing embodied-AI startup participating in the fair, has signed a 500-million-yuan (about 74.66 million U.S. dollars) deal with green-tech group Envision, and the first batch of its K15 semi-humanoids arrived at Envision's battery gigafactory in France this month for autonomous loading and unloading work. But the machines are only part of the business. The training and the services that keep them working overseas are increasingly where China's services trade will lie in the future. The fairground tells the same story. The information and communications technology (ICT) hall alone featured more than 30 debut products, from high-jumping and cooking robots to wall-climbers and holographic cabins. "Visitors can feel an intelligent economy where carbon-based (humans) and silicon-based (robots) beings coexist," said He Qionghua, head of the ICT exhibition area. Back at the calligraphy booth, the "fu" is a blessing for visitors, while the fortune it points to is increasingly being created by robotic hands. ■

item.title: Smart technologies power high-quality development of China's mining industry
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-14
TIANJIN, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- At the exhibition booth of Unissky (Nanjing) Technology Co., Ltd., a four-legged inspection robot moved steadily, autonomously adjusting its movements when encountering obstacles and following predefined routes. Designed for inspection in confined and hazardous spaces such as underground mines, the robot drew the attention of many visitors to the 2026 China Mining Conference and Exhibition. "This product is primarily designed for confined and hazardous environments such as underground mines, and it has broad application potential in the mining sector," said Xu Tao, a solution manager at Unissky. The global mining industry is undergoing a profound digital transformation. In recent years, China has embraced smart technologies to modernize its mining industry, with digital twins, autonomous mining, and AI-powered exploration gaining ground across operations. China's push for smart mining is helping drive the industry into a new stage of development. The coal industry offers a glimpse of this transformation. By the end of 2025, China had 1,066 intelligent coal mines, with intelligent production capacity accounting for more than 65 percent of total coal production capacity, according to data from the China National Coal Association. Artificial intelligence is being rapidly adopted across the coal industry, with applications spanning production and operations, safety management, and equipment maintenance. Autonomous driving technology is also gaining ground in open-pit mines. In China, more than 4,000 autonomous mining trucks were in operation by the end of 2025, according to industry statistics. In 2024, seven Chinese government departments jointly issued the guiding opinions on advancing the construction of intelligent mines and promoting the safe development of mines. The document calls for establishing a comprehensive system covering technology, equipment and management for smart mining by 2030, with greater integration and broader sharing of mining data. Ren Shoumai, an official at the China Geological Survey, said geological mapping is like drawing a "geological navigation map" for the subsurface mineral world. On Friday, the Ministry of Natural Resources unveiled an AI-powered mineral exploration system, AI-OreSeeking, and an AI-powered geological mapping system, AI-GeoMapping, aiming to reshape geological survey workflows and provide a new technological paradigm for global mineral exploration. AI-GeoMapping has been widely trialed on nearly 100 1:50,000-scale geological map sheets in Qinghai, Xizang, Xinjiang, Fujian, and other provincial-level regions of China, and has also been promoted in Morocco, Saudi Arabia, Laos and other countries. It identifies geological bodies with overall accuracy exceeding 90 percent and improves the efficiency of data processing, integrated analysis and geological map compilation by more than 50 percent compared with traditional methods. Experts attending the event said cutting-edge technologies such as artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things and 5G have become increasingly integrated into the entire mining lifecycle, driving breakthroughs in areas such as smart mine development and mining machinery manufacturing. At Huangling Mining Co., Ltd., a subsidiary of Shaanxi Coal and Chemical Industry Group, production data at the No. 1 Coal Mine are updated in milliseconds on screens at the surface dispatch and command center. Folds in rock layers and variations in coal seam thickness that were previously difficult to observe are now converted into 3D visual data through smart technologies, enabling more precise prediction and dynamic control of underground operations. At Yidong Group's Lijiata Coal Mine, a high-precision personnel positioning system and a 5G-based communication and dispatch system have created an underground high-speed information network, significantly improving mine safety management and emergency response. At Qinglong Coal Mine, operated by Guizhou Qianxi Energy Development Co., Ltd., intelligent shearers equipped with memory cutting and automatic following, as well as intelligent roadheaders featuring inertial navigation, laser positioning and infrared remote control, are being used in mining operations. These technologies have significantly reduced the physical workload of workers while boosting production efficiency. "Mining robots are helping enable unmanned operation at fixed workstations and robotic operations at hazardous posts," said Wang Lin, a marketing manager at CITIC HIC Kaicheng Intelligence Equipment Co., Ltd. The company's coal-gangue sorting robot on display at the conference uses big-data-based intelligent recognition technology to automatically identify and separate coal from gangue, helping mining companies improve sorting efficiency and operating returns, Wang said. Smart mining practices are also being extended to other fields. During the construction of a reservoir bridge in Macheng, central China's Hubei Province, the project team of China Railway 18th Bureau Group Co., Ltd. applied smart technologies to key construction processes and independently developed a range of tools, including a precision positioning device for embedded sleeves in track slabs. These innovations have helped address long-standing challenges such as significant positioning deviations in traditional manual operations, significantly improving construction quality and precision. Wang Sufeng, deputy director and secretary-general of the Smart Mine Professional Committee of the China Association of Work Safety, said smart mining is key to developing new quality productive forces and enhancing workplace safety, and is an essential path to the industry's high-quality development. Looking ahead, experts said the industry needs to improve intelligent decision-making and inter-system coordination, build centralized data platforms to enable data sharing, and accelerate the development of technologies for transparent geological information and safer, more energy-efficient power systems. Industry insiders called for closer cooperation among government agencies, mining companies, equipment manufacturers, universities and research institutes to advance smart mining and inject new momentum into the industry's high-quality development. ■
